name: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
objectives: Without notes, explain in plain words what artificial intelligence and generative AI are and why AI can sound sure and still be wrong, in two or three sentences that use the ideas of patterns and guesses

Given a simple example such as a spam filter, describe how an AI learns from data and how poor or one-sided data leads to biased answers, naming the examples, the patterns and one way the guesses could be unfair
Using your own phone or computer, identify at least five places where you already use AI and find one setting that controls it, with five correct examples and one setting opened
Using a free AI assistant, write a clear prompt that says what you need, the situation and how you want the answer, with all three parts and no private information
Given a first answer from an AI assistant, improve the answer with follow-up requests and check its facts on an official or trusted source, with at least two follow-ups and at least one fact checked

Before you send a prompt or use AI-written words, check the prompt for private information, follow the rules on AI help and respond safely to AI-powered scams, with every private detail replaced by a placeholder and the right safe action chosen every time

lessons.title: Lesson 1: AI in plain words
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Explain in two sentences what artificial intelligence is.
This lesson builds toward: Without notes, you will explain in plain words what artificial intelligence and generative AI are and why AI can sound sure and still be wrong, in two or three sentences that use the ideas of patterns and guesses.
Artificial intelligence (AI) means computer programs that do tasks that usually need a person: understanding speech, recognizing a face in a photo, suggesting a song, translating a sentence, or writing an answer to a question.
AI does not think or feel like a person. It is very good at finding patterns in huge amounts of examples and using those patterns to make a guess. A good guess can look smart; a bad guess can look just as confident.
There are many kinds of AI. The kind people talk about most today is generative AI: tools like ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot and Google Gemini that generate (make) new text, pictures or sound when you ask.
Words to know:
- Artificial intelligence (AI): computer programs that do tasks that usually need a person, like understanding speech or answering questions.
- Pattern: something that repeats in a way you can predict.
- Generative AI: AI that makes new text, pictures or sound when you ask it.
Try it now: Without looking back, say or write two sentences that explain AI to someone who has never heard of it. Use the words "patterns" and "guess".
You can now explain in plain words what AI is and why it can be wrong.

check.q: In this course, what does generative AI do?
options: It only sorts emails into folders
It makes new text, pictures or sound when you ask
It thinks and feels like a person
It always knows the true answer
check.why: Generative AI tools like ChatGPT, Copilot and Gemini generate new text, pictures or sound.

check.q: A friend says, "The AI sounded so sure, so it must be right." What would you tell them?
options: That is true; AI is never wrong when it sounds sure
Only paid AI tools can be wrong
AI makes guesses from patterns, so a wrong guess can sound just as confident
AI is only wrong when the internet is slow
check.why: AI uses patterns to make a guess, and a bad guess can look just as confident as a good one.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: How AI learns from examples
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Describe how an AI learns, using a simple example.
This lesson builds toward: Given a simple example such as a spam filter, you will describe how an AI learns from data and how poor or one-sided data leads to biased answers, naming the examples, the patterns and one way the guesses could be unfair.
Most AI today learns from examples instead of from rules a person types in. To teach a program to spot spam email, people show it many emails that are marked "spam" or "not spam". The program finds the patterns, like certain words or strange links, and uses them on new emails.
The examples it learns from are called data. Good, varied data makes better AI. If the data is old, one-sided or missing some groups of people, the AI's guesses will be old, one-sided or unfair too. This is called bias.
Writing tools like ChatGPT learned from a huge amount of text, so they are good at predicting which words should come next. That is why they write smoothly, and also why they can write something that sounds right but is not true.
Step by step:
- People collect many examples (data).
- The program looks for patterns in the examples.
- It uses the patterns to guess about something new.
- People check the guesses and give it better examples when it is wrong.
Words to know:
- Data: the examples, numbers, words or pictures an AI learns from.
- Bias: when the data leans one way, so the AI's guesses are unfair to some people.
- Training: the step where an AI learns patterns from data.
Try it now: Think of something you learned from examples, like telling ripe fruit from unripe fruit. Write how you would teach a computer the same thing: what examples would you show it, and what might it get wrong?
You can now describe how AI learns from data and why poor data leads to poor or unfair answers.

options: Guesses that lean one way because the data was old, one-sided or missing some groups
A setting that makes the AI faster
A type of computer virus
A way to make the screen brighter
check.why: When the examples are one-sided or missing groups of people, the AI's guesses become unfair too.

check.q: You want to teach a program to tell ripe fruit from unripe fruit. What would you do first?
options: Type one rule and hope it works
Show it a single photo of a banana
Tell it to guess with no examples
Show it many photos of fruit, each marked ripe or unripe
check.why: AI learns by finding patterns in many marked examples, called data.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Spotting AI in your day
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Find at least five places where you already use AI.
This lesson builds toward: Using your own phone or computer, you will identify at least five places where you already use AI and find one setting that controls it, with five correct examples and one setting opened.
You probably use AI every day without calling it that. Your phone's map picks a faster route around traffic. Your email moves junk into a spam folder. Video and music apps suggest what to watch next. Your phone unlocks with your face. Your keyboard suggests the next word.
Voice assistants such as Siri, Google Assistant and Alexa use AI to understand what you say. Banks use AI to spot card payments that look unusual. Job websites use it to match your résumé to openings.
Knowing where AI is helps you ask good questions: why did the app suggest this? Can I turn it off? What does it know about me? Most apps have settings where you can see or change this.
Words to know:
- Voice assistant: an AI you talk to out loud, like Siri, Google Assistant or Alexa.
- Recommendation: a suggestion an app makes based on what you or people like you chose before.
Try it now: Look through your phone or computer and list five places that use AI. For one of them, open its settings and find one choice you can change.
You can now spot AI in the tools you use every day and find settings that control it.

check.q: Which of these uses AI to understand what you say?
options: A paper calendar
A desk lamp
A voice assistant such as Siri or Alexa
A printed bus timetable
check.why: Voice assistants use AI to understand speech.

check.q: A music app keeps suggesting songs you do not like and you wonder what it knows about you. What would you do?
options: Delete your phone
Open the app's settings to see or change what it uses
Stop listening to music
Type your password into the search box
check.why: Most apps have settings where you can see or change how suggestions work.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Asking an AI assistant for help
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Open a free AI assistant and write a clear, three-part prompt.
This lesson builds toward: Using a free AI assistant, you will write a clear prompt that says what you need, the situation and how you want the answer, with all three parts and no private information.
Free AI assistants include ChatGPT (chatgpt.com), Microsoft Copilot (copilot.microsoft.com) and Google Gemini (gemini.google.com). They work in a web browser or as an app from the official app store.
What you type is called a prompt. A clear prompt has three parts: what you need, a little about the situation, and how you want the answer. For example: "I run a small church food pantry. Write a friendly 4-line message asking for Saturday volunteers. Use simple words."
A one-word prompt like "volunteers" makes the AI guess what you mean, so the answer is general and less useful.
Step by step:
- Open an AI assistant in the browser or the official app.
- Say what you need.
- Add the situation, without private details.
- Say how you want the answer: length, list, steps, simple words.
- Send it and read the answer.
Words to know:
- Prompt: what you type or say to an AI assistant to ask for something.
- AI assistant: an AI program you chat with by typing or talking, such as ChatGPT, Copilot or Gemini.
Try it now: Open one free AI assistant. Write a three-part prompt for a real task this week, such as a birthday message, a study plan or a shopping list, and send it.
You can now open a free AI assistant and write a clear prompt that gets a useful first answer.

options: What you type or say to an AI assistant
A warning from your phone
The AI's answer
A type of password
check.why: The prompt is what you give the AI assistant to tell it what you need.

check.q: You need a short birthday message for your aunt. Which prompt would you send?
options: "Birthday"
"Write something"
"Message"
"Write a warm 3-line birthday message for my aunt, who loves gardening. Use simple words."
check.why: It says what you need, the situation and how you want the answer.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Improving and checking the answer
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Improve an answer with follow-ups and check its facts.
This lesson builds toward: Given a first answer from an AI assistant, you will improve the answer with follow-up requests and check its facts on an official or trusted source, with at least two follow-ups and at least one fact checked.
Treat the first answer as a draft. In the same chat you can ask: "Make it shorter." "Use simpler words." "Give me three choices." "Put it in a table." The assistant remembers the earlier messages in that chat.
AI can make things up: a wrong date, a phone number that does not exist, an old rule. This is called a hallucination. Check any fact about money, health, law, benefits, dates, addresses or phone numbers on an official website (US government sites end in .gov) or with a person who knows, like a doctor, librarian or case manager.
Ask the assistant "Where can I check this?" and then go to that site yourself.
Step by step:
- Read the first answer.
- Ask for one change at a time.
- Underline the facts: numbers, dates, names, rules.
- Check each fact on an official or trusted source.
- If they differ, trust the official source.
Words to know:
- Follow-up: a second message that asks the AI to change or explain its answer.
- Hallucination: when an AI writes something that sounds true but is made up.
Try it now: Take your answer from the last lesson. Ask for two changes, one at a time. Then pick one fact in it and check it on an official or trusted website.
You can now improve an AI answer with follow-ups and check its facts before you use it.

check.q: What is a hallucination in AI?
options: When the AI runs out of battery
When the AI refuses to answer
When the AI makes up something that sounds true
When the AI answers in another language
check.why: AI can make up a wrong date, number or rule that sounds right; that is a hallucination.

check.q: An AI answer gives the date a benefits form is due. What would you do before you rely on it?
options: Check the date on the official website or with a person who knows
Trust it because it came from AI
Ask the AI the same question again and use that
Share it with friends first
check.why: Facts about dates, money, benefits and rules should be checked on an official source.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Using AI fairly and safely
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use AI without sharing private information and in a fair, honest way.
This lesson builds toward: Before you send a prompt or use AI-written words, you will check the prompt for private information, follow the rules on AI help and respond safely to AI-powered scams, with every private detail replaced by a placeholder and the right safe action chosen every time.
Do not type private information into an AI assistant: Social Security or ID numbers, passwords, bank or card numbers, medical record numbers or a full home address. Write "[my number]" instead. Your chats may be stored by the company.
Be honest about AI help. Many schools and jobs have rules about it, so ask before you hand in AI-written work. Read and change what it writes so it sounds like you and says what you mean.
Remember bias: if an answer seems unfair to a group of people, question it. And watch for AI-powered scams, such as fake voices of family members asking for money. Stop, hang up, and call back on a number you know.
Step by step:
- Read your prompt for private information before you send it.
- Replace private details with a placeholder.
- Check your school's or job's rules on AI help.
- Make the final words your own.
- Treat rushed money requests as a warning sign.
Words to know:
- Private information: details that could let someone pretend to be you or take your money.
- Placeholder: a stand-in like "[my number]" that you write instead of the real detail.
Try it now: Final task: pick a real task, write a clear prompt with no private information, ask for two improvements, check one fact on a trusted website, then explain AI to a friend in three sentences.
You can now use AI to finish a real task while keeping private information safe and using it honestly.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Explaining AI The explanation is missing, wrong, or does not say why the answer was checked. Three plain sentences say what AI is, that it guesses from patterns, and why the answer was checked. Also gives an everyday example and mentions that poor data can make answers unfair. Clear prompt The prompt is one or two words or misses what is needed. The prompt says what you need, the situation and how you want the answer. The prompt also sets a length or format and gets a useful first answer. Improving the answer No follow-up was asked, or the first answer was used as it was. Two follow-ups were asked, one at a time, and the answer got better. The final words were also changed so they sound like you. Checking a fact No fact was checked, or it was checked only by asking the AI again. One fact was checked on an official or trusted website. Every fact about dates, money, rules or phone numbers was checked, and any difference was fixed. Privacy and honesty The prompt contains a private detail such as an ID number, password or full address. The prompt has no private information; any personal detail is a placeholder. Also checked the school's or job's rules on AI help where they apply. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Why should you keep private information out of an AI chat?
options: It makes the answer longer
AI assistants cannot read numbers
It is against every school's rules
Your chats may be stored by the company
check.why: The company may keep your chats, so ID, bank and medical numbers should never go in.

check.q: You get a call in your grandson's voice asking you to send money right now. What would you do?
options: Send the money quickly
Hang up and call him back on a number you know
Give your bank card number to check it is him
Ask the caller to send a text instead
check.why: AI can copy voices, so stop and call back on a number you already know.
